extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and applicants before the German Patent and Trade Mark Office (DPMA); patent attorneys and practitioners involved in German patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on examining patent applications under the German Patent Act, covering patentability (inventive step, industrial application), search and amendment practice, unity/division rules, claim drafting and priority. Intended to direct examiners' practice and inform applicants of procedural/substantive requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires that the skilled person, with his knowledge and skills, was able to develop the subject matter of the invention from the known state of the art and must have had reason to choose the solution according to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment assumes the known art gave the skilled person a reason or suggestion to arrive at the proposed teaching. Decisions in comparable cases only serve as guidelines; whether an invention involves an inventive step depends on the individual case. The skilled person assessed is the developer of the subject matter, not the user. Examiners must avoid retrospective reasoning and treat the subject matter as part of their knowledge at the filing/priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of known art as a suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: A new technical teaching is not to be regarded as lacking an inventive step merely because there are no grounds that would constitute an obstacle in reaching it from the known state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key question is whether the known art suggested the solution; mere absence of obstacles does not prove lack of inventiveness. If known art provides a suggestion to arrive at the proposed teaching, that supports obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: General expert knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that forms part of the general expert knowledge may provide a reason to use a solution, but being part of general knowledge alone is not sufficient proof that it was obvious to use that knowledge in solving a particular technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General suitability of a solution in many applications is only sufficient if it is immediately clear to the skilled person that a technical starting point exists where use of that solution seems objectively suitable. Context and special circumstances must be identifiable that make other applications impossible or difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary indicia for inventive step (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as overcoming technical prejudices, futile efforts of experts in the past, satisfaction of a long-standing need, simple and low-cost manufacturing, reduction of production costs, or synergistic effects can be indicative of an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These auxiliary criteria may only, in individual cases, give grounds for a particularly critical review; however, if such auxiliary criteria are merely aggregated from known features in an obvious way, they do not establish inventiveness. Random or arbitrary selection from known alternatives is not suitable to establish an inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of certain prior publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications having an earlier filing or priority date but made available to the public on or after the date governing the filing/priority date of the later application are not to be considered for assessing inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty and inventive step, only prior art available before the relevant date is considered (reference to section 4 sentence 2 of the Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic assessment of claim features
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment of the claim must always be based on the combination of all features, regardless of whether the claim is formulated in one or two parts; isolated consideration of individual features is not admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the claim as a whole; do not split the claim into separate analyses of single features when evaluating inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider only instructions influencing the technical solution
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining inventive step, only those instructions are to be taken into account which determine or at least influence the solution of the technical problem by technical means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-technical or purely administrative teachings that do not affect the technical solution should not be treated as part of the state of the art for inventive-step purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination the assessing body must treat the subject matter as already part of its knowledge when deciding whether the invention was obvious at the filing or priority date; otherwise the approach would be retrospective and impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must place themselves in the position of the skilled person at the relevant date and not use later-acquired insights to judge obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application (capability of industrial application)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is capable of industrial application if its subject matter can be manufactured or used in any field of industry, including agriculture; i.e., it is possible to manufacture the subject matter in an industrial enterprise or make technical use of it in an industrial enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a low threshold: practical manufacture or technical use in an industrial context suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search scope in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The search is carried out to identify the relevant state of the art to assess whether the filed invention is patentable; the subject matter of a search is the invention given in the patent claims; the description and drawings are used to interpret the claims; the search covers all independent and dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examining section in charge of the main class is responsible for the search. Ensure claims are properly interpreted using description/drawings and search all claim scope including dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search methods, tools and termination
rubrics_metrics.description: The examining section must carry out the search utilising the technical tools and information sources made available to the extent that seems promising and justified, considering effort and time requirements; the search is concluded where disproportionate effort would be required to only slightly improve results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Guidelines for the Search under Section 43 (use of external electronic sources). To avoid unnecessary procedural delay, carry out and finalise the search in one working step for all claims before the first communication. Beware searches done before six months after filing may be erroneous due to incomplete availability in systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's duty to disclose known prior art upon request
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant does not indicate the concrete state of the art in his application documents, he must, on request of the Office, indicate the state of the art known to him and include it in the description (section 34 (7) of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply may affect examination; applicants should provide known prior art when requested to facilitate search and examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party submissions during search/examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications that might prejudice the grant of a patent may be indicated by a third person not party to the procedure and must, as a rule, be forwarded to the applicant ex officio together with accompanying documents as soon as possible after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such third‑party publications will be taken into consideration ex officio in subsequent examination. Forward them promptly to applicants to ensure efficient handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and prohibition of extension (no added subject‑matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original application documents may be amended up to the decision on grant provided that the scope of the subject matter is not extended; only corrections of obvious mistakes, remedying deficiencies pointed out by the examining section, or amendments to the patent claims are admissible before filing a request for examination. Section 38 prohibits amendments that extend scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unallowable extensions are not removed, the application must be refused. Carefully check that amendments are directly and unambiguously derivable from the original documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of original disclosure (what counts as disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the original application is what the average skilled person can infer from the original documents as belonging to the invention applied for; disclosure only includes what was capable of being derived directly and unambiguously from the documents originally filed and does not comprise more extensive knowledge obtained by the skilled person's general expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the overall content from the perspective of the same skilled person who assesses patentability. Unallowable extension occurs if subject matter becomes apparent only via the skilled person's own considerations beyond the original documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'comprise' versus 'consist'
rubrics_metrics.description: If it can be inferred from original documents that a product is meant to 'comprise' certain components, it is not automatically disclosed that no further components may be added; to show that a product 'consists' exclusively of stated components, additional clues in the original documents are generally necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit indications (advantages or desirability) if exclusivity is intended; otherwise interpret in the inclusive 'comprise' sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention (prohibition of multiple inventions in one application)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must not relate to more than a single invention or a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (section 34 (5) of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine lack of unity, the examiner must assess whether, considering technological context and clarity, processing in different procedures seems appropriate. A lack of unity objection must be well-founded; even if lack of unity is apparent without reference to the state of the art, patentability of the subject matter must be substantively commented on and the art taken into consideration stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division due to lack of unity (declaration requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where lack of unity is found, the examining section invites the applicant to establish unity either by issuing a declaration of division due to lack of unity or by abandoning the lacking part; the declaration must clarify what remains in the parent application and the divisional must not go beyond the disclosed content of the parent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If declaration ambiguous, invite clarification within a fixed time; absence of clarification leads to refusal. Divisional arises upon receipt of declaration and becomes independent while continuing at the procedural stage of the parent at time of division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and fee consequences for divisional applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications are treated like regular applications: fees (application, examination, renewal) apply; the filing/priority date of the original continue to apply; the amount and due date of fees depend on form of filing and number of claims, with specified payment windows and consequences for non-payment (withdrawal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination fee due within three months from the due date if a request for examination was filed for the parent. Non-payment can deem the divisional withdrawn (or the declaration of division deemed not made) with procedural consequences and possible loss of ability to claim divided subject matter in the parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of documents and time limits in divisional procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: In the procedure of the divisional application the applicant must file new documents as in the parent procedure; failure to file within time limits fixed by the examining section leads to refusal. Previous procedural acts in the parent case file are also part of the divisional case file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely file required documents and pay applicable fees; procedural history follows to divisional file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free division (voluntary division) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant may at any time divide his application by written declaration until expiry of the time limit for lodging an appeal against the decision to grant the patent (section 39 (1)); the filing date/priority date of the original application continue to apply to each divisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear declarations of division warrant a short time limit to clarify; required documents must be filed and fees paid within three months or the declaration is deemed not made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent claims form and drafting (one‑part and two‑part form)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must contain one or more patent claims defining the subject matter sought; claims may be drafted in one-part form or divided into a generic part and a characterising part (two-part form). The characterising part must include the features of the invention for which protection is sought in connection with the generic part and be preceded by wording such as 'characterised in that'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In two-part form the generic term is usually formed from one document or subject matter made available to the public. The entire claim (generic + characterising parts) must be examined; there is no substantive difference between one-part and two-part forms for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims determine scope of protection and drafting balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 14 the content of the patent claims determines the scope of protection; matter merely presented in the description and not clearly claimed is not protected. The inventive idea should be described abstractly to comprise all embodiments desired by applicant, subject to original disclosure and state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, weigh applicant's interest in broad protection against public interest in clarity. Use the description to interpret the claim, but avoid unnecessary features in the main claim; define the subject matter with as few characteristics as possible to avoid undue narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main claim essentials and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The main claim must contain the essential features of the invention. The main claim may be followed by subsidiary (dependent) claims relating to particular embodiments, admissible provided the principle of unity is complied with. Sub‑claims involving a change of category must be examined separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the main claim captures the core inventive concept; dependent claims may cover specific embodiments but must remain within unity and proper claim category treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process and purpose/function indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are admissible (especially for chemical compounds not identifiable structurally). Indications concerning purpose, effect or function used to designate a device are not inadmissible and often necessary to establish clear connection of structural characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose/function language usually does not limit subject matter to the stated purpose but indicates the device must be objectively fit for that purpose. Such indications help the skilled person determine how to design features spatially and geometrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional/embellishing claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional features such as 'in particular', 'preferably' or 'for example' are permissible in claims; they do not limit the claimed subject matter and are not relevant for substantive patent examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such phrasing as non-limiting; examination focuses on the features that define the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim category classification and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may concern products (devices, apparatus, substances) or processes; the objectively evaluated subject matter determines the patent category and thus limits free choice of claimed category by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including features of different categories in a single claim to maintain unambiguous IP rights. For manufacturing processes, claims must contain the original material and chronological sequence of actions; use claims are classified as process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic priority claiming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority of earlier German applications for the same invention may be claimed provided the later application is filed within 12 months and a domestic/foreign priority has not already been claimed for the earlier application (section 40 (1)). The declaration of priority must be made together with the file number of the earlier application within two months from the filing date of the later application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier application is still pending when priority is claimed, it is deemed withdrawn as soon as the declaration is submitted. For PCT cases, deemed withdrawal may occur after a 31‑month time limit; examining section may process the earlier application or wait.
